```{r library}
library(conductoR)
```

## Who sees what

A plan is often written by someone who never sees the data: a composer,
human or automated, sends the plan to the data holder, the holder runs it,
and only a return comes back. This vignette follows one run from the table
the holder checks before anything runs to the report the composer writes
afterwards. Five steps, each a function of the package:

1. the table is checked against the plan's postconditions (`conduct()`)
2. the return carries more values as its dose rises (`run_return()`)
3. each value is checked on its own before it leaves (`default_checker()`)
4. values that could be solved from one another are withheld together
   (`suppress_return()`)
5. every number in the report is traced to a value of the return
   (`trace_report()`)

## The data and the plan

`agridat::hernandez.nitrogen` holds 136 maize plots from a 2006 trial at
five Minnesota sites, four replicates per site, at nitrogen rates from 0 to
268 kg/ha (Hernandez and Mulla 2008). Yield is in t/ha. Site S5 has 24 plots,
the other sites 28.

```{r data}
data("hernandez.nitrogen", package = "agridat")
d <- hernandez.nitrogen
table(d$site)
```

One tool fits the response of yield to nitrogen, across all plots and at
each site. The site estimates go in the manifest's `params` table, one row
per site with its plot count.

```{r tool}
fit_response <- function(inputs, data, node) {
  fit <- lm(yield ~ nitro, data = data)
  slope <- unname(coef(fit)["nitro"])
  n <- nrow(data)
  by_site <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(data, data$site), function(s) {
    data.frame(site = as.character(s$site[1]),
               slope = unname(coef(lm(yield ~ nitro, data = s))["nitro"]),
               mean_yield = mean(s$yield),
               n_plots = nrow(s))
  }))
  m <- lens_to_manifest(
    "effect", slope > 0, emitter = "maize", method = "maize:ols",
    metrics = list(slope = structure(slope, n_units = n),
                   slope_per_100 = structure(100 * slope, n_units = n),
                   mean_yield = structure(mean(data$yield), n_units = n)))
  m@params <- by_site
  m
}
```

The plan declares two things beyond its node. The input `data` must have
136 rows, no negative rate, and one row per site, replicate and rate. The
node declares what it may return: the overall values at dose 1, the site
rows at dose 2, each with its unit and its significant figures. A site row
rests on the plots in its `n_plots` column.

```{r plan}
plots <- plan_input("data", key = c("site", "rep", "nitro"),
                    postconditions = c(P_rows = ".n_rows == 136",
                                       P_rate = "nitro >= 0"))
per_kg <- "t/ha per kg N/ha"
plan <- oap_plan(
  id = "maize_nitrogen",
  meta = list(question = "How does maize yield respond to nitrogen?"),
  inputs = list(plots),
  nodes = list(node(
    "fit", fit_response, emits = "treatment_effects",
    returns = list(
      list(field = "slope", dose = 1, unit = per_kg, digits = 3),
      list(field = "slope_per_100", dose = 1, unit = "t/ha", digits = 3),
      list(field = "mean_yield", dose = 1, unit = "t/ha", digits = 3),
      list(field = "params.slope", dose = 2, unit = per_kg,
           n_units_field = "n_plots", digits = 3),
      list(field = "params.mean_yield", dose = 2, unit = "t/ha",
           n_units_field = "n_plots", digits = 3)))))
plan_returns(plan)
```

## Step 1: the table is checked before anything runs

A table that breaks a postcondition stops the run before the first node.
The error names the condition and how many rows fail, never a value.

```{r postconditions}
broken <- d
broken$nitro[3] <- -33.6
msg <- tryCatch(conduct(plan, data = broken, verbose = FALSE),
                postcondition_failed = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
cat(msg)
```

The real table passes, and the run goes ahead.

```{r run}
run <- conduct(plan, data = d, verbose = FALSE)
run$postconditions[, c("input", "id", "holds")]
```

## Step 2: the dose sets how much comes back

At dose 0 the return is the record of the run and its typed message alone.
Every requested value is listed as refused, with the reason `above_dose`.

```{r dose0}
requests <- plan_returns(plan)
ret0 <- run_return(run, dose = 0, requests = requests)
ret0$lines
ret0$refused
```

At dose 1 the overall values come back. The site rows still need dose 2.

```{r dose1}
ret1 <- run_return(run, dose = 1, requests = requests)
ret1$values
ret1$refused
```

## Step 3: each value is checked before it leaves

At dose 2 the site rows are requested too. The checker refuses any value
resting on fewer than `k` units, here `k = 25` plots. A `params` field is
checked row by row, so S5's row, on 24 plots, is withheld and the other
four are returned. The refusal counts the withheld rows and does not name
them.

```{r dose2}
ret2 <- run_return(run, dose = 2, requests = requests,
                   checker = default_checker(k = 25))
ret2$values[ret2$values$field == "params.mean_yield", ]
ret2$refused
```

## Step 4: a withheld value must not follow from the released ones

Withholding S5's mean yield is not enough. The overall mean is the
plot-weighted mean of the five site means, so S5's mean can be solved
from what was returned:

```{r route}
site <- aggregate(yield ~ site, data = d, FUN = mean)
site$site <- as.character(site$site)
n <- as.vector(table(d$site))
solved <- (sum(n) * mean(d$yield) - sum(site$yield[1:4] * n[1:4])) / n[5]
all.equal(solved, site$yield[5])
```

`suppress_return()` looks across the cells of a release for such routes.
The holder declares that the five sites partition the whole. What the
released sites leave of the whole is then one withheld site, so one more
site is withheld to break the route.

```{r suppress}
cells <- data.frame(node = "fit", field = "mean_yield",
                    unit = c("all", site$site),
                    value = c(mean(d$yield), site$yield),
                    status = c(rep("released", 5), "withheld"),
                    n_units = c(sum(n), n))
parts <- data.frame(parent = "all", child = site$site)
res <- suppress_return(cells, partitions = parts, k = 25)
res$changes[, c("unit", "status", "rule")]
res$cells[, c("unit", "status")]
```

With two sites withheld, the released values give their combined mean but
neither one alone. The check finds only the routes it is told about, here
the declared partition, and those it searches for by itself.

## Step 5: every number in the report traced to the return

The composer writes the report from the return. A value is written as a
reference, `{{<node>:<field>}}`, and `trace_report()` fills it in. Any
number written out must match a value of the return at the digits shown,
or be declared in `allow` as not a result, such as the plot count or a
nitrogen rate.

A number the composer worked out for itself does not trace, and the report
is blocked. Here the draft gives the gain from a 150 kg/ha dressing, a
number the run never computed:

```{r trace_blocked}
draft <- c(
  "Across 136 plots, yield rose by {{fit:slope}} t/ha for each kg/ha of",
  "nitrogen, so a 150 kg/ha dressing added about 3.5 t/ha. Mean yield was",
  "{{fit:mean_yield}} t/ha.")
blocked <- trace_report(draft, ret1, allow = c(136, 150), run = run)
blocked$released
blocked$trace[blocked$trace$status == "untraced",
              c("line", "shown", "status", "reason")]
```

A number the report needs in another form is computed in the run, so that
it too is a value of the return. The tool already returns the gain per
100 kg/ha as `slope_per_100`, and the report refers to it instead.

```{r trace_released}
report <- c(
  "Across 136 plots, yield rose by {{fit:slope}} t/ha for each kg/ha of",
  "nitrogen, about {{fit:slope_per_100}} t/ha per 100 kg/ha. Mean yield",
  "was {{fit:mean_yield}} t/ha.")
traced <- trace_report(report, ret1, allow = c(136, 100), run = run)
traced$released
cat(traced$text, sep = "\n")
traced$trace[, c("shown", "status", "node", "field", "value")]
```

The trace carries the plan and input hashes of the return, so every
number in the released report points back to one run of one plan on one
table.

## Reference

Hernandez, J. A., & Mulla, D. J. (2008). Estimating uncertainty of
economically optimum fertilizer rates. *Agronomy Journal*, *100*(5),
1221–1229. <https://doi.org/10.2134/agronj2007.0273>
